patterns: how to write a good flashcard
entries.answer: A flashcard puts one question on one side and one answer on the other, and the whole method depends on you trying to answer before turning it over. Used that way it is a form of self-testing, which is why it works far better than reading a list of facts aloud. Used the other way, flipping through cards you already know, it becomes re-reading in a more expensive form. The design rule is one idea per card, and a card asking what are the three causes of the war will fail every time.

entries.answer: Revision is going over material you have already studied, and the word covers everything from a five-minute look the night before to a full re-do of a term's work. The reason the night-before version feels effective is that familiarity is easy to mistake for recall, and the two are not related. Revision is worth doing in the sense that it finds gaps, and it is not worth doing as a way of feeling more confident, since confidence is the one thing reading reliably produces.

patterns: how to make a mind map
entries.answer: A mind map puts a central idea in the middle with branches radiating out, and the value is that it forces you to decide what belongs where, which is a harder task than listing. That classification is the useful part; the drawing is not, and an hour on the layout is an hour not spent on the material. It works best as a reconstruction rather than a copy, so you map from memory and then check, and a map made by copying the chapter is a decorated outline.

patterns: how to elaborate on an idea
entries.answer: To elaborate is to add a connection or an example to something you already half know, and it works because the new material is attached to something existing rather than stored alone. This is why explaining a concept to somebody else is such a reliable test, since the gaps show up in the explanation rather than the knowledge. The trap is adding detail that is easy and not detail that matters, so a long explanation of the mechanism is not the same as understanding why it is asked.

patterns: how to mix topics when revising
entries.answer: Interleaving is mixing different topics in one practice session rather than blocking each one separately, and it feels harder and works better. Blocking, where all the fractions are done then all the decimals, produces a high score during practice and a poor one later, because the skill being tested is recognising which method applies. Interleaved practice is less comfortable and produces better retention, which is an uncomfortable combination that students consistently under-choose.
